content.title: About
content.content: Potato french fries are sliced potatoes that are blanched, flash‑frozen, and ready for frying. When cooked they become crispy with a golden exterior and a soft interior. The product is widely used in fast‑food restaurants and home kitchens.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first commercial french fries appeared in the United States in the early 20th century.
Freezing preserves the flavor and texture of the fries for several months.
Different countries serve fries with a variety of sauces: ketchup, mayonnaise, tartar sauce, etc.
There are “shoestring” and “steak‑cut” cuts, each offering distinct culinary qualities.

items.title: Source of potassium
items.content: Potatoes are rich in potassium, which supports normal heart and muscle function.

items.title: Vitamin C
items.content: Fresh potatoes contain vitamin C, though much of it is lost during frying.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: Potatoes provide fiber that aids digestion.

items.title: High fat content
items.content: Frying adds significant calories and saturated fats to the fries.

items.title: Acrylamide formation
items.content: High‑temperature cooking can produce acrylamide, a potentially harmful compound; avoid over‑cooking.

items.title: Salt
items.content: Fries are often salted, which may be a concern for people with hypertension.

content.title: How to Cook
content.content: Heat oil to 175‑180 °C (350‑356 °F). Add frozen strips and fry for 3‑5 minutes until golden and crisp. Drain on paper towels, season with salt to taste, and serve hot.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep frozen french fries in a freezer at –18 °C or lower. After opening, use within 3‑4 months. Do not thaw before frying.
